introduction: These few readings ask in what sense a Manifestation of God exists before His birth. ‘Abdu’l-Bahá distinguishes stations: the body and the rational soul have a beginning; the Word of God, which shines in them, has none, and that is not incarnation. The language is that of John’s prologue and of Proverbs on Wisdom, which stand here beside the readings, along with the verses over which Christians and others have argued about what “before” can mean, and two poets who gave every soul a life before birth.
questions: “Before Abraham was, I am.” How do the three stations of the second reading explain who is speaking?
John says the Word was made flesh; the sixth reading says the divine nature is not transformed into the human. Is the difference one of doctrine or of language?
Wordsworth and Plato give every soul an existence before birth. What do the last readings say of ordinary souls, and why does the difference matter to them?

outside.why: The reality of Christ “precedes all created things”. His own sentence, in a tense that grammar cannot place: before Abraham was, I am.
The Word of God is “sanctified beyond time”. The prologue of John is the source of the phrase and of the thought: in the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God.

The third station, the Word and Holy Spirit, “hath neither beginning nor end”. Wisdom in Proverbs speaks in the first person of the same priority: the Lord possessed me in the beginning of his way, before his works of old.
Paul gives that station to Christ in one line: he is before all things, and by him all things consist.

The body and the rational soul have a beginning; the Word shines in them. John’s verse joins what the reading keeps apart: the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us. Does “made flesh” say more than the reading allows, or the same in an older idiom?
God’s Manifestation in creation “hath neither beginning nor end”. The voice in the Revelation of John: I am Alpha and Omega, the beginning and the ending.
The hymn praises a primal Sea, Morn, Sun and Fire. Milton, invoking Light, hesitates between the same two ways of speaking: offspring of Heaven firstborn, or of the Eternal coeternal beam.
“When thou didst believe in God before creation.” Jeremiah hears of himself what the Báb says here to a believer: before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee.

Bahá’ís “do not believe in the incarnation of the Word”. The verse most pressed in the other direction: I and my Father are one, for which the hearers took up stones, because that thou, being a man, makest thyself God. What kind of oneness do the readings affirm, and what kind did the hearers suppose?

Before He sits on it a throne is only “the work of” a craftsman, and few see more. Nazareth saw only the craftsman’s household: is not this the carpenter’s son? is not his mother called Mary? What would they have had to see?

“The Prophets, unlike us, are pre-existent.” Wordsworth gave the prior life to every child: our birth is but a sleep and a forgetting; trailing clouds of glory do we come from God, who is our home. What do the readings keep for all souls, and what do they reserve?
